prompt: Instead of 'add an export button', the ticket says 'accountants need the numbers in their spreadsheet'.
tells: accountants need the numbers in their spreadsheet
why: Describing the user's problem leaves room for better solutions. Start from the need.
trap: Asking why might get you there, but the clue is how the need is written.

prompt: As a parent, I want to see homework due this week, so that I can help on time.
tells: so that I can help on time
why: A user story states the need and the benefit.
trap: It names the user, but the core is the need.

prompt: The request said 'build a chatbot', but the problem was customers couldn't find the returns page.
tells: customers couldn't find the returns page
why: The real need was simpler than the requested solution. Start from the need.
trap: Asking why found it; the lesson is need over solution.

prompt: The team watches nurses work for a day to see what slows them down.
tells: to see what slows them down
why: Watching users find their real problems is understanding the need.
trap: It identifies users, but the aim is their needs.

prompt: The interview asks, 'What's the most annoying part of booking a room today?'
tells: the most annoying part of booking a room today
why: Asking about pain points uncovers needs.
trap: It isn't about scope; it's finding the problem.

prompt: A long feature list doesn't say what problem any feature solves.
tells: doesn't say what problem any feature solves
why: Features without needs miss the point.
trap: Sorting comes later; first link features to needs.
